title: HTA annual report lands, and a contamination refresher
metaDescription: The HTA's 2025 to 2026 annual report, a practical refresher on cell culture contamination, and three smaller items for people who look after samples.
whyThisMatters: The HTA's annual report is the regulator's own account of the year, and the place to read what inspections found before your own next visit.
Contamination in cell culture is still a leading cause of lost work, and the controls are mostly habits, not equipment.
Digital pathology and organoid research keep raising the bar for how tissue and derived material are documented.
bodyHtml:
A quieter fortnight than most, with one regulator publication that deserves a slow read and a useful practice piece on contamination. Here is what moved and what it means for people who look after samples.

The HTA publishes its annual report and accounts for 2025 to 2026

The Human Tissue Authority published its annual report and accounts for 2025 to 2026 on 20 October 2026. The document is the regulator's formal account of its year, laid before Parliament, and it is the one place where licensing, inspection and enforcement activity across all of the HTA's sectors is summarised together.

What it means for sample custodians: read the sections on inspection findings and on the regulator's priorities for the coming year, and compare them with your own last inspection report. Where the HTA says it is focusing attention, that is a reasonable guide to what a Designated Individual will be asked about next.

Three habits make an annual report useful rather than just long. First, read it with your own licence conditions open beside it, so that each theme the regulator raises can be checked against something you already do. Second, note any figures the regulator gives for shortfalls and the standards they fall under, and ask whether the same standard would hold up at your establishment today. Third, record what you decided to change as a result, with a date, because the next inspector will want to see that the report was read and acted on, not just filed. None of this takes more than an afternoon, and it is the cheapest preparation an establishment can do.

We will return to the report in a later issue once the full document has been read against last year's edition, so that the trends across the two years can be set out properly rather than guessed at from the summary.

Cell culture contamination: sources, detection and control

The Scientist has published a practical overview of cell culture contamination, covering where it comes from, how it is detected and what keeps it out. The piece is written for bench scientists, but the controls it describes are the same ones a tissue bank or a research facility relies on every day.

What it means for sample custodians: contamination events are rarely about one bad day. They come from routine, so the useful response is to look at the routine: how often lines are tested, how incoming material is quarantined, and whether the record of each test is kept with the sample it relates to. A complete record of what was tested and when is what lets a team show, later, that a problem was contained rather than spread. Pro-curo's audit trail exists for exactly this kind of question.

Digital pathology tool separates tumour DNA from healthy tissue

Also in The Scientist, a new digital pathology tool is described that masks healthy tissue on a section so that tumour DNA can be isolated more cleanly. The detail comes from the article summary.

What it means for sample custodians: as analysis of archived sections becomes more targeted, the value of a section depends on knowing exactly which block, which patient consent and which processing history it came from. Tools like this reward collections that have kept that chain intact.

Organoid study shows microglia recruiting T cells

An eLife paper describes an integrated human forebrain organoid in which microglia mediate the recruitment of CD8 positive T cells. It is basic research, and the detail here comes from the published summary rather than the full paper.

What it means for sample custodians: organoid work depends on well characterised starting material. Facilities supplying cell lines and tissue for this kind of study are increasingly asked for provenance and consent records at the point of request, not after publication.

On our radar

  • A molecular typewriter maps cell lineages in mice: a new lineage tracing method, reported by The Scientist.
  • Bruce suppresses autophagy-regulated caspase activity in Drosophila: developmental biology from eLife, included for completeness.

That is the fortnight. If a regulator publishes a change to an obligation in the next two weeks, the following issue will be an explainer on that change rather than a briefing.
